claims.text: Rasmus Lerdorf released version 1.0, then called Personal Home Page Tools, on 8 June 1995, announcing it on the newsgroup comp.infosystems.www.authoring.cgi under the subject Announce: Personal Home Page Tools.

source.title: History of PHP — the project’s own account of the 1995 Personal Home Page Tools release and the rewrites that followed

claims.text: What was released was a set of small, tightly written CGI binaries in C — a utility library and templating mechanism rather than a scripting language. A complete rewrite followed in October 1995, and the second generation arrived in April 1996.

source.title: History of PHP — the project’s own account of the 1995 Personal Home Page Tools release and the rewrites that followed

claims.text: The name was originally an abbreviation of Personal Home Page, and was later redefined as a recursive abbreviation for Hypertext Preprocessor.

source.title: History of PHP — the project’s own account of the 1995 Personal Home Page Tools release and the rewrites that followed

claims.text: The model is that a file is a document which may contain code, rather than a program which emits a document: the page is served as written except where an escape into code occurs.

source.title: History of PHP — the project’s own account of the 1995 Personal Home Page Tools release and the rewrites that followed

beats.broke: producing a page that varied by request meant writing a program that printed the page, so the document lived inside the program as strings
beats.fix: invert it — the document is the file, and code is escaped into it where the page has to vary
beats.cost: the inversion puts logic wherever the output goes, so there is no structural boundary between what the page says and how it was decided
beats.interview: what the inversion actually buys, and why the property that made it spread is the property that made large ones unmaintainable
